comparisons.peer_topic: Noninterest expense increase drivers and prior year comparisons
comparisons.peer_summary: Noninterest expense increased $967 million to $66.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023, primarily driven by higher revenue-related expenses and investments in people, operations, and technology, partially offset by higher FDIC expense in 2023 (including a $2.1 billion special assessment) and lower expenses from a liquidating business activity.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and BAC disclose that their 2024 operating/noninterest expenses were significantly impacted by prior-year FDIC special assessment fees, though the net movement differed. GS reported a 2% decrease in operating expenses, citing 'significantly lower expenses, including impairments' and 'other significant expenses recognized in the prior year, including... the FDIC special assessment fee' as key drivers for the drop. Conversely, BAC reported a $967 million increase in noninterest expense, noting it was 'partially offset by higher Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) expense in 2023, including $2.1 billion for the estimated special assessment'. While both acknowledge the FDIC fee's role in the year-over-year variance, GS benefited from the absence of such charges in 2024 (along with CIE impairments), whereas BAC faced higher base expenses (compensation, technology) that overcame the benefit of lower FDIC charges in 2024.

sentences.text: Operating expenses were $33.77 billion for 2024, 2% lower than 2023, reflecting decreases driven by significantly lower expenses, including impairments, related to commercial real estate in consolidated investment entities (CIEs) and other significant expenses recognized in the prior year, including the write-down of identifiable intangible assets related to GreenSky Holdings, LLC (GreenSky), an impairment of goodwill related to Consumer platforms and the FDIC special assessment fee.
These decreases were partially offset by higher compensation and benefits expenses (reflecting improved operating performance) and higher transaction based expenses.

comparisons.comparison: JPM and GS both address the composition of their noninterest/operating expense changes in 2024, with compensation being a major upward driver for both. JPM's noninterest expense rose 5% to $91.8 billion, driven by 'higher compensation expense, including higher revenue-related compensation and growth in the number of employees'. GS similarly noted that its decreases were 'partially offset by higher compensation and benefits expenses (reflecting improved operating performance)'. Both companies also highlight the impact of FDIC special assessments, though in opposite directions relative to the prior year: JPM noted 'lower FDIC-related expense' due to the timing of a $2.9 billion assessment in 2023 versus a $725 million increase in 2024, while GS cited 'FDIC special assessment fee' as part of the significant expenses recognized in the prior year that decreased in 2024.

Similarly, GS reported a 2% decrease in total operating expenses, driven in part by 'other significant expenses recognized in the prior year, including... the FDIC special assessment fee'. While MS reports an increase in expenses driven by compensation (formulaic payouts), both peers explicitly cite the reduction in FDIC assessment costs as a favorable variance driver against the prior year's higher charges.
